```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# No need to run this chunk unless you're "knitting"
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE,
                      comment= NA, 
                      warning = FALSE,
                      message = FALSE)
```


Load `tidyverse` package using the `library` function.

```{r}
# Load tidyverse
library(tidyverse)
```


Load our data. 

```{r}
# Load the data
d_blomkvist <- read_csv("../../data/blomkvist.csv")
```

What aesthetics and attributes can be used depend to the geometry (although there will be overlap across geometries). For example bring up the documentation of `geom_point` by running

```{r eval = F}
?geom_point
```

and find the section called "Aesthetics". This section will tell you that for `geom_point` there are the following aesthetics you can use to render data as dots:

- x
- y
- alpha (i.e. opacity)
- colour
- fill
- group
- shape
- size
- stroke

Required are `x` and `y`. They must be used as aesthetics. Most of the remainder (not `group`) can be used as either aesthetics or attributes.

Let's start by using attributes. Again, many attributes like `alpha`, `colour`, `fill` exist for all geometries. We will start with points as an example. 

Attributes take properties. The number of options for many of these properties, and certainly their combinations, is virtually unlimited. So here are just a few examples how to change and combine them.

For example, change the size of the points to 5.

```{r}
ggplot(d_blomkvist, aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d)) +
  geom_point(size = ---)
```

Instead of using dots we can display other types of shapes. The following code that generates an overview of `ggplot2`'s standard shapes that can be used as aesthetics and attributes. So if you want dots to be rendered as a triangle you could set `shape` to `2`. 

```{r}
# Specify numbers from 1 to 25 which represent shapes 
shapes <- 1:25

# Create a data frame with locations for all 25 shapes
data <- tibble(x = rep(1:5, 5),
               y = rep(1:5, each = 5),
               shape = shapes)

# Create a plot that shows these shapes along with their identifiers.
ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(shape = factor(shape)), size = 5) +
  geom_text(mapping = aes(label = shape), nudge_y = -.25) +
  theme_void() +
  coord_trans(y = "reverse") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = shapes) +
  theme(legend.position = "nope")
```

Complete the following code to render the data as squares with a cross inside.

```{r}
ggplot(d_blomkvist, aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d)) +
  geom_point(shape = ---)
```

You could also render dots as all sorts of other symbols such as "$", "%", "£", etc., just set the `shape` argument to the symbol for dollar in inverted commas to render the data as dollar symbols.


```{r}
ggplot(d_blomkvist, aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d)) +
  geom_point(shape = ---)
```


and many other ways to render data as [emojis](https://jtr13.github.io/cc21fall1/icons-and-symbols-in-r.html) and other [images](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2019/09/using-emojis-and-png-as-icons-in-your-ggplot/).


You can then go ahead and change the colour of these dots. For example, try to change the dots to blue by adding the property "blue" to `colour`, or any other colour.

```{r}
ggplot(d_blomkvist, aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d)) +
  geom_point(colour = ---)
```

There are many colours and colour schemes available for `ggplot2`. See for example [here](https://r-graph-gallery.com/ggplot2-color.html).


Shapes 21 to 25 in the overview above are empty shapes that allow you to add the `fill` option. All other shapes can't be filled. For example, fill shape 21 with blue. Try to use shape 1 just so you see that it won't have an effect.

```{r}
ggplot(d_blomkvist, aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d)) +
  geom_point(shape = ---, fill = ---)
```

Now this doesn't look different from just using the colour attribute and the default shape. The point of having a different attribute for colour and fill is that you have the option to use a different colour for their outline and their centre. 

In addition you can combine other attributes too. Complete the following code to render the data as triangles of size 3.5 with purple outlines and red filling.

```{r}
ggplot(d_blomkvist, aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d)) +
  geom_point(size = ---, colour = ---, shape = ---, fill = ---)
```




Once you've completed all tasks above you can `knit` this document to HTML.
